claims.text: The as-synthesized Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles are single-phase solid solutions with nominally uniform bulk composition.
The nanoparticles may contain local variations in atomic arrangement.
Rapid quenching promotes enhanced local short-range chemical order in these nanoparticles.
Slow cooling produces a more homogeneous atomic distribution than rapid quenching.
Local short-range chemical order produces regions with variable bonding strengths.
Enhanced short-range order creates clusters with lower local cohesive energy than a homogeneous solid solution.
Lower local cohesive energy reduces the activation-energy barrier for atomic diffusion.
Low-cohesive-energy ordered regions serve as nucleation sites for premelting.
Enhanced short-range order causes premelting to begin at lower temperatures.
Enhanced short-range order causes premelting to evolve in a spatially heterogeneous manner.
Rapidly quenched nanoparticles will have a broader premelting regime than slow-cooled nanoparticles.
Rapidly quenched nanoparticles will have a lower premelting-onset temperature than slow-cooled nanoparticles.
The earlier onset of premelting will appear as early contrast changes in HRTEM.
Slow-cooled nanoparticles will exhibit a relatively well-defined and higher premelting-onset temperature.
The proposed mechanism applies to 10–20 nm Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles under inert or vacuum conditions while the solid solution is maintained.
Significant oxidation or other extrinsic chemical changes may invalidate the proposed relationship between short-range order and premelting.
Statistically indistinguishable premelting onsets and spatial melting behavior despite confirmed differences in local order would falsify the hypothesis.
